commenti.body: I love film but I’ve never heard of Hal Hartley or any of his films. I’d be intrigued to know what to start with. I love women’s films if perhaps he has one. Do you have a suggestion? I’m definitely intrigued!

Henry Fool is a very interesting movie, but it didn't quite work for me in the end.
I still think Trust is his best work. 

However Hal Hartley was pretty much considered a legend of indie cinema in the 90s, even more so than Stillman (even though his movies were a lot more polished).

I recently watched Henry Fool, the only film of his I've seen. I have similar feelings to Ebert. It feels like I should like it, I can sense an endearing playfulness in Hartley's style. He has a humorous/cynical worldview that I appreciate. At the same time it feels like there isn't much substance, thoughtful characterization/dramatization, things go weird in a way that feels kind of forced or even lazy attempts at provocation. I don't know, just kind of ambivalent about it, and the unpleasant elements slightly outweigh the positives to me.
Have you seen the other two in the trilogy?

It's been years since I watched his films but oh yeah do I have thoughts: I didn't take to his style too fondly, but I would say he kind of laid the groundwork for the dry, emotionless approach to how actors behave in Wes Anderson films along with maybe...Noah Baumbach as well? The actors in Hartley, like Anderson films, talk in narrative forms about their existence as if they are outside themselves, making statements about their existence. 

I always come close to liking his work but in the end, I actually feel more depressed and irritated than inspired when I'm done watching his films. He, along with Anderson, have to find a way out of the stale maze they create for their movies. I like that they make that choice but they have to find that engine or motor that keeps the plot going because character development is definitely not a strong suit in their films, so a strong,funny plot needs to be there and a lot of the times it isn't since the films of Hartley or Anderson always resort back, especially with Hartley, to a character or characters waxing some philosophical rant in the middle or end of the film.

I'm no expert on the films of Hal Hartley, as I said, but I think *Henry Fool* can be read as a pretty harsh critique of just this. The title character is a self-obsessed, self-proclaimed genius who creates elaborate aesthetic/philosophical justifications for his selfish, antisocial and even criminal behavior. I certainly don't think the film presents his rants at face value.

_Trust_ made a huge impact on me when I saw it, when I was around sixteen. I’m not sure why, but I didn’t feel that kind of Brechtian distancing effect after like 2 minutes. The characters seemed to be expressing themselves more directly, more fully than typical characters; they avoided the kind of caricaturing that happens in regular movies and the subterfuge used by people in real life. That’s how it came across.

[This scene](https://youtu.be/li70Z-3GMlk?t=17m) is a good example (not sure about the whole video).

But I suppose I was on his wavelength at the time. I had similar reactions to some Godard, Truffaut, and most especially _La maman et la putain_. Stillman’s pretty close, though Wes Anderson never quite clicked with me in the same way. Age of exposure might be a factor.

If you weirdly do happen to click with early HH, the best distillation IMHO is a 60 minute shorter work called Surviving Desire. That’s got Martin Donovan’s best performance, though again, it is very stagy. 

Post Henry Fool or so, his movies have clicked with me less, though I continue to watch with interest.
Would you recommend *The Unbelievable Truth*?

I think you just said it. His closest thing to a traditional hit was Henry Fool which, despite featuring a known name like Parker Posey, was still decidedly arthouse. Add to that his prime coming before the internet and his films not being quite revolutionary enough to get packed in with Linklater, Tarantino, or even a lesser indie force like Kevin Smith circa Clerks (which itself seemingly has a few Hartleyisms in it) and yeah—he was never going to become a household name.

I don't know the age range of the posters on this, but I think Hartley was an auteur for his time and place. I was in grad film school back in '89 and our prof James Schamus (the writer/producer/exec) brought in Hartley to class (Schamus was a producing partners with Ted Hope, who produced Hartley's early works) just before the release of The Unbelievable Truth.  We watched it and I remember it being quite the idiosyncratic experience.  It felt fresh and novel.  Yes, the Brechtian vibe and the Godardian vibe.  At the time, though, you had folks like Jarmusch, Whit Stillman, Soderbergh, and even Todd Haynes who had just come out with his Karen Carpenter experimental piece.  So, there was this palpable new wave coming out of the New York scene especially.  Much of it was formulated on post-modern, ironic styles and deadpan humor, and it was highly popular (for an indie scene) at the time.  Hartley had a good run in the 90s for those of us who were part of that audience back then.  His films got picked up and were distributed by reputable companies (Miramax, Fine Line, Sony Pictures Classics).   He peaked IMO with Henry Fool which was the consummate distillation of his style.  But, I do think he was a filmmaker for his time and place and really part of that film culture back then.  And perhaps that iconoclasm hasn't translated will after the 2000s.  I wonder if millennials would "get" his early works watching them now for the first time.

Trust was a revelation to me when it was released: it felt incredibly fresh and bold and quite inspiring. I've since seen other work that likely influenced it (e.g. by Bresson, Pinter, Brecht), but I watched it again a few years ago and it holds up very well. The final scene (no spoilers!), and the way the musical theme that has been very discreetly building throughout finds a glorious, exuberant climax, was still hugely powerful.

The Unbelievable Truth is also excellent - but it feels a bit diluted compared to Trust, as if Hartley hadn't yet found the confidence to follow some of his ideas to their logical conclusion (e.g. that very stilted style of dialogue).  Simple Men was very accomplished too, but lacked the freshness of Trust. In the subsequent 2 or 3 films, I started to find the Hartley style - once so distinctive and bold - mannered rather than stylised, and the narrative oddities contrived rather than intriguing. I felt he was a victim of his own originality - like "difficult third album" syndrome in moviemaking. But at one point in time, his was a unique vision in American cinema, in my opinion, and I'm sure it was very influential on other "indie" filmmakers of the time, most of whom have gone on to much "bigger things" (whether that be a measure of success or not) than Hartley.   


I wish him well and would love to see him develop a TV series.

He hasn't made a film in nearly 10 years. As I said above, I do wonder if he became something of a prisoner of his own style...
